newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr firmer, but rally and data indecisive.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr firmer, but rally and data indecisive.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a grip on modest gains at midday but dealers were loth to try anything more meaningful in the face of offshore offers around US$0.7630.

There was some relief the Reserve Bank did not ease this morning, as some had feared, and also that March quarter GDP data were not so weak as to get the money markets slavering for an immediate cut. The average measure of GDP rose 0.9 percent on the quarter against forecasts of a 0.8 percent gain.
Annual growth still slowed sharply to 2.4 percent, however, from more than 3.0 percent in Q4 and the GDP price deflator was benign enough to keep a policy easing on the agenda.
By 12.15 pm (2215 GMT) the local dollar was holding at US$0.7610/15 having crept up to an early US$0.7606/11 from US$0.7595/00 late Tuesday and a low of US$0.7560.

It did pop as high as US$0.7630 this morning after the RBA stayed silent at its 9.30 am operation, confounding speculation it had decided to ease at its monthly board meeting on Tuesday. Analysts always thought it unlikely it would move so soon after the May 23 cut, but have been surprised by the RBA before.
But there was no follow-through buying and the currency quickly retreated, suggesting it was far too early to say the two-week downtrend from US$0.7770 had found bottom.
Traders said it would be hard for the currency to sustain any sort of rally while the risk of a domestic rate cut hung over it and, for that matter, the risk of a U.S. hike.

Today's GDP data were not decisive for the domestic rate question since those looking for another easing could point to more recent figures showing weakness, such as April retail trade data last Friday.

Nevertheless, the GDP rise of 0.9 percent was a relief to dollar bulls as market estimates had ranged as low as 0.25 percent. The slowdown in annual growth was also exaggerated as a unusually large 1.7 percent gain from Q1 last year dropped out.

Treasurer Peter Costello was also keen to emphasise that an unexpected dive in business inventories had taken a chunk out of GDP growth in the quarter. It would only take stocks to stay steady in Q2 to contribute around 1.0 percentage point to GDP growth, he noted.

However, he also pointed to subdued price indicators in the report -- the GDP-E deflator rose a mild 0.3 percent on the quarter and 1.6 percent on the year -- and said there indications on wages growth showed it was not in a danger zone for policy makers. Analysts took all that as meaning there could be scope on the inflation front to ease again if necessary.

Costello also noted that Australian manufacturers would be pleased with the recent decline in the dollar. He emphasised the government had no target level for the currency, but analysts reckoned he did not sound displeased with the fall either.

Some had thought the fall in the dollar this year, of more than five percent in trade weighted terms, would argue against another easing since its strength last year had played a large part in keeping inflation down.
The net result of all this was that another cut could not be ruled out or in and the dollar would remain hostage to every piece of economic data in the foreseeable future.
On the crosses the local currency was range-bound on the yen at 88.48/58 from 88.30/40 late Tuesday, much in line with US$/yen which was dithering around 116.00 yen.
It was firmer on the mark at 1.3154/66 from 1.3067/80 as the German currency continued to suffer from doubts over both the timing and credibility of European monetary union.
In tare weighted terms the dollar edged up to 58.0 from 57.9 late Tuesday.
The next event of note for the domestic market would be a speech by RBA governor Ian Macfarlane at a conference in London on Thursday. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1818
